Shroud
SHROWD
n. (a shelter of foliage; a covering that shades)
Hebrew choresh, a wood or thicket — here the dense canopy of a great tree. Old English scrud, a garment or covering. The now-dominant sense of a burial cloth is later English; the biblical use is arboreal.

Biblical Definition

Behold, the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon with fair branches, and with a shadowing shroud, and of an high stature; and his top was among the thick boughs. Ezekiel is warning Pharaoh by describing what happened to somebody greater, and the figure is a magnificent tree. The shroud is its canopy — the shadowing cover of foliage that made it a shelter for everything beneath. The prophet develops that shelter at length and generously: all the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs, and under his branches did all the beasts of the field bring forth their young, and under his shadow dwelt all great nations. Assyria genuinely did provide order and protection over a vast territory, and Ezekiel says so. Then he names the fault, and it is one word: height. Because thou hast lifted up thyself in height, and he hath shot up his top among the thick boughs, and his heart is lifted up in his height — therefore the sentence follows. The tree is given into the hand of the mighty one of the heathen and cut down. Nothing in the passage condemns greatness as such; God made the tree, and the chapter says elsewhere that he made it fair. What is condemned is a greatness that has become conscious of itself, in which the heart rises with the stature. Nebuchadnezzar, who is the intended audience of the warning through Pharaoh, later supplied the line that says it perfectly: Is not this great Babylon, that I have built by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): that which clothes, covers or conceals; shelter; a cover; the dress of the dead; a branch or covering of foliage.

SHROUD, n. That which clothes, covers, conceals or protects; a garment; shelter; cover.

SHROUD, n. The dress of the dead; a winding sheet.

SHROUD, n. A branch of a tree; hence, a covering or shelter of foliage.

CANOPY, n. A covering over a throne, or over a bed; a covering spread over the head.

STATURE, n. The natural height of an animal body; bulk; size; eminence.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 31:3 — "Behold, the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon with fair branches, and with a shadowing shroud, and of an high stature; and his top was among the thick boughs."

Ezekiel 31:6 — "All the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs, and under his branches did all the beasts of the field bring forth their young, and under his shadow dwelt all great nations."

Ezekiel 31:10 — "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thou hast lifted up thyself in height, and he hath shot up his top among the thick boughs, and his heart is lifted up in his height;"

Daniel 4:30 — "The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?"

Modern Corruption

National and personal greatness is treated as self-generated achievement; Ezekiel grants the greatness, credits God with it, and identifies the fall with a heart lifted up in its own height.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is uncontested; the principle to recover is Ezekiel's diagnosis of how great powers fall. Modern accounts of imperial decline reach for economics, overextension, or internal division, and those things are real second causes that Scripture nowhere denies. But Ezekiel places the decisive fault in the heart of the thing: his heart is lifted up in his height. That is a claim about providence — that God raises and casts down nations, and that pride is the condition under which he casts them down. Daniel says the same in plain doctrine: the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will.

The passage is also notably generous, which is what makes it useful rather than merely severe. Ezekiel does not pretend Assyria was worthless. The tree was fair, the canopy really did shelter nations, and the birds and beasts really did live under it. Christians commenting on their own nation, institution, or work would do well to imitate the balance. It is possible to acknowledge genuine good achieved under a power that God is about to humble, and Scripture does it in the same paragraph as the sentence. What is not possible is to keep the greatness and lose the ascription. The moment a man says the might of my power and the honour of my majesty, the tree is already marked.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew choresh (H2793), a wood or thicket; erez (H730), a cedar; tsel (H6738), a shadow; gabah (H1361), to be high or lifted up.

expand to see more

Hebrew choresh (H2793) — a wood, a thicket; rendered shroud, of the tree's canopy.

Hebrew erez (H730) — a cedar; the figure for Assyria, and the glory of Lebanon.

Hebrew tsel (H6738) — a shadow; under his shadow dwelt all great nations.

Hebrew gabah (H1361) — to be lofty, to be exalted; the fault named at verse 10.

Hebrew leb (H3820) — heart; what was lifted up along with the height.

Usage

"“with a shadowing shroud” — the canopy that sheltered nations."

"“under his shadow dwelt all great nations” — the greatness granted."

"“his heart is lifted up in his height” — the fault identified."
